Introduction

[
1
]

This matter is currently proceeding under an
amended petition filed December 29, 2022 by Akm Harun-ar-Rashid as Petitioner
with the British Columbia Commissioner for Teacher Regulation as the Respondent.
As will be discussed in further detail below, the petition also designates the
Board of School District No. 35 (the “Langley School District”) and Trish
Kolotyluk as “on notice”.

[
2
]

I will refer to Akm Harun-ar-Rashid as the
“Petitioner” and Mr. Rashid in these Reasons. At a Case Planning Conference on
April 4, 2023 in front of Master Robertson, Mr. Rashid advised that was his
preferred reference for court purposes.

[
3
]

The Langley School District and Trish Kolotyluk
each bring applications to, generally, clarify that they each have no role in
the underlying petition and to remove them from the proceeding. The Langley
School District also applied for an order pursuant to
s. 18
of the
Supreme
Court Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 443, precluding the Petitioner from
instituting any further legal proceedings without leave of the Court. Both
applicants also sought an order for costs in their favour.

History of the Matter

[
4
]

This matter has a significant history which
predates this petition proceeding. I will briefly trace the events that led to
this proceeding. In total, as against the Teacher Regulation Branch, Mr. Rashid
has sought judicial review of a Teacher Regulation Branch certification
requirement, brought a claim before the British Columbia Human Rights Tribunal
alleging the certification requirement was discriminatory, sought judicial
review of that Human Rights Tribunal decision, pursued reconsiderations and
appeals from teacher regulation entities, and brought the underlying petition.

[
5
]

Additionally, Mr. Rashid brought a claim against
the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and 12 other defendants, in the Court of
King’s Bench of Alberta. That claim was dismissed and is discussed in detail
below, beginning at para. 16.

Proceedings Against the Teacher
Regulation Branch

Judicial Review: English Language
Proficiency Requirement

[
6
]

In April 2018, Mr. Rashid applied for a teaching
Certificate of Qualification from British Columbia’s Teacher Regulation Branch.
As a requirement of the certification process, Mr. Rashid was required to
provide evidence of English language proficiency. Mr. Rashid refused to do so,
and instead filed a petition for judicial review on October 2, 2018. That
application was heard and dismissed by Mr. Justice Jenkins on November 9,
2018 for the reasons as essentially set out in the Teacher Regulation Branch’s Response
to Petition. The primary reason for dismissal—beyond Jenkins J.’s concerns
about Mr. Rashid’s pleadings—was that Mr. Rashid’s application was premature as
no decision had actually been made by the Teacher Regulation Branch in Mr.
Rashid’s application for certification.

Human Rights Tribunal

[
7
]

Mr. Rashid then filed a complaint with the
British Columbia Human Rights Tribunal against the British Columbia Ministry of
Education, Teacher Regulation Branch on January 14, 2019. In that proceeding,
Mr. Rashid submitted that a requirement to provide an acceptable score on an
English proficiency test constituted discrimination against him based on his
ancestry, colour, place of origin, and race in violation of
s. 8
of the
Human
Rights Code
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210. The Teacher Regulation Branch denied
discrimination, submitting that the requirement was based on the Certification
Standards that require teachers be proficient in the language of instruction
(English or French). The Teacher Regulation Branch evaluator assigned to Mr. Rashid’s
case had been concerned about the quality of his written and oral communication
based on his communications with the evaluator, and not on any of the protected
characteristics. The evaluator reported these concerns to the Director of
Certification, who then required Mr. Rashid to provide evidence of English
language proficiency. The evaluator reported this requirement to Mr. Rashid,
who refused to believe the evaluator, and took the position that the evaluator
must be discriminating against him and had “intentionally added the language
requirement to delay [his] certification”.

[
8
]

The complaint was dismissed with written reasons
on June 8, 2021:
Harun-ar-Rashid v. Ministry of Education (Teacher
Regulation Branch)
,
2021 BCHRT 75
[HRT Decision]. Given the circumstances
in which Mr. Rashid had refused to provide evidence of English language
proficiency, the certification process had stalled and no determination in the
certification process had yet been made with respect to issuance of a teaching
certificate. The Human Rights Tribunal dismissed the complaint as premature
pursuant to
s. 27(1)
(c) of the
Human Rights Code
, as the complaint had
no hope of proving discrimination.

[
9
]

The Human Rights Tribunal specifically found
that there was no reasonable prospect that Mr. Rashid could prove that the
requirement for demonstrated English language proficiency was a pretext for
discrimination or that it negatively affected his ability to obtain a teaching
certificate in B.C. The Human Rights Tribunal noted that the Teacher Regulation
Branch had made its decision “without regard to his ethnicity”, and only on Mr.
Rashid’s individual characteristics on their merits. The Human Rights Tribunal (“HTR”)
further opined that even if Mr. Rashid could prove the underlying elements of
his complaint, that the Teacher Regulation Branch would be reasonably certain
to justify the language proficiency standard as a
bona fide
reasonable
justification.

Judicial Review: Human Rights
Tribunal Decision

[
10
]

Then, in August 2021, Mr. Rashid filed a
petition for judicial review of the HRT Decision. The respondent, the Teacher
Regulation Branch applied for an order that the petition be struck out in its
entirety pursuant to Rule 9-5 of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
, B.C.
Reg. 168/2009 [
Rules
]. The petition was heard
by
Mr. Justice Edelmann with reasons provided on May 20, 2022:
Harun-ar-Rashid
v. British Columbia (Human Rights Tribunal)
,
2022 BCSC 965
[Judicial Review
of the HRT Decision].

[
11
]

At para. 8 of his decision, Edelmann J.
characterized Mr. Rashid’s claims as “a laundry list of orders that are either
not available by way of petition, not properly brought together with any
judicial review, not within the jurisdiction of this court or have no entry or
legal foundation”. Edelmann J. then criticized the nature of Mr. Rashid’s
petition:

[10]

The Petition
itself freely mixes facts, speculation and bare assertions with legal arguments
and attacks on the character of groups or individuals. It is replete with
wholly unsupported allegations against various individuals and organizations
that I have little hesitation in describing as scandalous or vexatious. This
includes a number of allegations against the evaluator who is accused of
“perjury”, as being part of a “master plan of discrimination” and one of a
group of Asian Canadians “used as the shield of the discriminatory actions” by
the [Teacher Regulation Branch]. The Petitioner goes on to plead that “Those
Asian Canadians do not hesitate to commit perjury when a complaint is brought
to the court assuming that the ministry would save them.” These types of
completely unsupported, scandalous and vexatious statements have no place in
pleadings before this Court and filing them is, without question, an abuse of
this Court’s process.

[
12
]

Ultimately, Edelmann J. struck Mr. Rashid’s
pleadings based on the following conclusion:

[13]      Neither
in the Petition, nor in many hours of argument before me, was the Petitioner
able to point to any evidence that was before the Tribunal to support the
theory that the evaluator was biased based on ethnicity. In effect, in this
Court the Petitioner had developed a new theory which was based on
discrimination against teachers from other provinces. This theory was not
raised before the Tribunal. In my view, the Petition does not articulate a
reasonable claim for judicial review of the BCHRT decision.

[
13
]

Edelmann J.’s decision was upheld in the Court of Appeal:
Harun-ar-Rashid
v. British Columbia (Human Rights Tribunal),

2023 BCCA 276
.

The Underlying Petition

[
14
]

In the midst of the proceedings at the Human Rights Tribunal and
before the courts, Mr. Rashid advanced an internal review process with the
Teacher Regulation Branch. The internal process led to a decision by the
Director of Certification to deny a Certificate of Qualification to Mr. Rashid
on August 17, 2021. The Petitioner requested a reconsideration of the denial
from the Director of Certification. On February 28, 2022, the Director of
Certification issued Reasons for Reconsideration, confirming the original
decision. On March 28, 2022, Mr. Rashid submitted an appeal to the Commissioner
of the reconsideration decision. On November 15, 2022, the Commissioner
provided reasons to the Petitioner, dismissing the appeal of the reconsideration
decision under
s. 71
of the
Teachers Act
, S.B.C. 2011, c. 19. It appears
that Mr. Rashid seeks judicial review of the decision to dismiss the appeal and
not to forward the decision to a review panel.

[
15
]

In December 2022, Mr. Rashid then brought the underlying petition in
this proceeding, ostensibly seeking relief under the
Labour Mobility Act
,
S.B.C. 2009, c. 20. The Petitioner reiterated this at the Case Planning
Conference held before Master Robertson on April 4, 2023.

Claim Against the RCMP

[
16
]

In the underlying petition, Mr. Rashid refers, at para. 18 of the
“Factual Basis” section, to an action which he commenced in Alberta against the
RCMP, among other defendants (the “Alberta Action”):
Harun-ar-Rashid v
Canada (Royal Canadian Mounted Police)
,
2019 ABQB 54
. Seven applicants
named as defendants in that action sought to strike out Mr. Rashid’s Statement
of Claim. The Alberta Action was heard by Mr. Justice Mandziuk J., who found
Mr. Rashid’s Statement of Claim disclosed no reasonable claim and that some
aspects were an abuse of process.

[
17
]

The Alberta Court dissected the Statement of Claim with some care,
highlighting Mr. Rashid’s allegations that the RCMP conducted a conspiratorial
investigation based on discriminatory grounds of race, ethnicity, colour and
perhaps others: at para. 35. At para. 39, the Court found that “on the most
liberal reading of the Statement of Claim”, redress for Mr. Rashid’s claim in
tort or other causes of action would only be available under the
Alberta
Human Rights Act
scheme; his claim before a civil court had no hope of
success before a civil court and was doomed to fail.

[
18
]

It would be an understatement to say that many of Mr. Rashid’s
allegations in the Alberta Action were outlandish. Commencing at para. 41 of
the decision, the Alberta Court conducted a detailed analysis of Mr. Rashid’s allegations,
which the Court found to be undetailed allegations against unnamed,
unidentified individuals claimed to be RCMP agents. The Alberta Court concluded
these allegations were incredible and did not merit a judicial response. The
Court also found that some of the claims were so fragmentary as to amount to vexatious
claims such as “an allegation that the RCMP maintains a blacklist of teachers,
on a racial basis, that is located in a ‘secret office at a remote abandoned
school building in a hilly forest area in Toronto’”: at para. 46.

[
19
]

Other outlandish claims in the Alberta Action, found to be without
substance or merit and struck as an abuse of process, included:

a)

allegations made against a non-existent police department;

b)

allegations that half-naked students in his classroom were wearing
body cameras and were RCMP collaborators;

c)

claims against the administration of several school districts where
no cause of action was made out; and

d)

a claim for a failure of a teacher’s association to represent the Petitioner
when he was not a member of the association.

[
20
]

Mandziuk J. concluded that while he struck the Statement of Claim on
other grounds, he could have also done so by classifying the litigation as a
vexatious proceeding: at para. 91. Mandziuk J. referred to thirteen categories
or indicia of abusive litigation which are grounds to strike out an action:
Chutskoff
v. Bonora
,
2014 ABQB 389
, aff’d
2014 ABCA 444
;
DKD (Re) (Dependent
Adult)
,
2018 ABQB 1021
.

[
21
]

Ultimately, Mandziuk J. provided the following
reasoning on whether Mr. Rashid’s litigation was vexatious:

[92]      Conservatively, the Plaintiffs’
litigation exhibits two of these indicia: 1) hopeless proceedings, and 2)
unsubstantiated allegations of conspiracy, fraud, and misconduct. Each of those
is also a basis on which I may strike out the Statement of Claim as a
vexatious, abusive proceeding. Here, both indicia categories are present, as I
have explained, and constitute separate bases to also strike out the Statement
of Claim.

[
22
]

In deciding to award elevated costs against Mr.
Rashid, the Alberta Court found that Mr. Rashid’s claims were—in many respects—hopeless,
vexatious and an abuse of the court. In closing, Mandziuk J. issued the caution
to Mr. Rashid:

[100]

In light of his
engaging in litigation which is vexatious and an abuse of court processes, I
caution the Plaintiff that if he continues to engage in litigation such as this
before this Court he may find himself subject to elevated cost awards and made
subject to prospective court access restrictions as a vexatious litigant.

[
23
]

Unfortunately, as the underlying petition and the hearing before me
in this case demonstrate, Mr. Rashid has failed to heed Mandziuk J.’s caution.

The Underlying Petition and
Applications

The Underlying Petition

[
24
]

The Petitioner seeks nine orders. In each of the first four orders
sought, the Petitioner seeks relief in relation to a decision made by the
British Columbia Commissioner for Teacher Regulation exercising authority under
the
Teachers Act
. While Mr. Rashid did not himself provide specifics on
that decision, it appears that he seeks judicial review of the Commissioner’s
decision to dismiss Mr. Rashid’s certification decision appeal rather than to
refer the certification appeal to a panel for a hearing.

[
25
]

In the fifth order sought, the Petitioner seeks orders (a) through
(g) inclusive to declare certain investigations or decisions of certain persons
invalid or unauthorized. In the sixth order sought, the Petitioner seeks,
without any reference to particulars or any factual basis, remedies under s. 24
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, Part I of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
, being Schedule B to the
Canada Act 1982
(UK), 1982, c. 11
[
Charter
].

[
26
]

Mr. Rashid designated the Board of Education of the Langley School
District and Trish Kolotyluk as “on notice” without naming either as parties in
the style of cause. According to Rule 1-1 of the
Rules
, a “party” means
“a person named as a party in the style of the proceeding”. Further, in his
petition under the heading “Orders Sought”, Mr. Rashid did not seek any order
or other relief against the “on notice” entities.

Applications “on notice”

[
27
]

The applications presently before the Court are brought by the “on
notice” entities: the Langley School District and Trish Kolotyluk. To
reiterate, neither of the applicants was included in the style of cause as
parties, nor as parties against whom the Petitioner sought any form of relief.

[
28
]

The Langley School District applies for an order clarifying that it
has no role in the underlying petition and that it be removed from the proceeding.
It also seeks an order striking paras. 24–32, 100, 103, and 117 from the
“Factual Basis” of the Amended Petition, and striking paras. 1, 15, and 21 from
the “Legal Basis” of the Amended Petition. The Langley School District seeks an
order precluding the Petitioner, as a vexatious litigant, from instituting
further legal proceedings without leave of court.

[
29
]

In the Amended Petition, Factual Basis, paras. 24 to 32 record the
Petitioner’s attempt, beginning in October 2018, to be hired as a teacher. This
attempt foundered because the Petitioner did not hold a valid teaching
certificate in British Columbia. In para. 100 of the same document, the Petitioner
seems to advance a claim under the
Charter
, followed by a legal opinion
under the
Labour Mobility Act
,
and a further opinion pursuant to the
School
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 412,

or
the
Independent School Act,
R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 216,

without any statement of fact. Paragraph 103 again refers
to an employee of the Langley School District allegedly breaching the
Charter
,
and seeks
Charter
relief. However, relief under the
Charter
is
not available in a proceeding by way of petition. Paragraph 117 again states a
legal opinion in which the Petitioner alleges he deserved special
consideration, pursuant to the provisions of the
Charter
, for
unspecified actions of five entities. This claim, apart from not being
available in a proceeding commenced by Petition, provides no particulars of the
conduct of any of the five entities, or any factual statement of actions by any
of the five entities referred to in that paragraph. There is also no indication
of whether these five entities acted individually or together. This claim has
not hope of success.

[
30
]

Like the Langley School District, Trish Kolotyluk also applies for an
order clarifying that she has no role in the underlying petition and that she
be removed from the proceeding. She also seeks an order striking paras. 46(k)
and 111 under the heading “Factual Basis”, without leave to amend. Ms.
Kolotyluk also seeks costs payable by Mr. Rashid.

[
31
]

Paragraph 46(k) refers to a letter written by
Ms. Kolotyluk dated November 12, 2020, which in full states:

Hi, Winson, when
I went further into the individual file I saw he had been inactivated in
December of 2018. I do not have current contact information for him nor would
he be able to gather reference letters from one of our schools as we discussed.

Should you be able to provide updated signed consent, we will gladly provide
with the documentation requested.

Trish Kolotyluk

Director, Human Resources, Consulting

Centre for Education

1 Kingsway NW, Edmonton, AB

[
32
]

As noted in a Memorandum dated November 23, 2020, Ex. I to the
affidavit of the Petitioner, p. 137, the authorization for Release of
Information from the Petitioner was not forthcoming and by email on November
12, 2020, the Petitioner advised he would not be providing a signed consent. In
a subsequent online conversation with Winson Ip, Ms. Kolotyluk “without
providing any personal or confidential information” (p. 138), advised that on
her review, she did “not believe that the file would contain anything that
would be concerning to the processes” of the Teacher Regulation Branch. In
other words, Ms. Kolotyluk did not provide any information about the Petitioner
to the Teacher Regulation Branch, and there is therefore no allegation against
her which would be the basis for relief, assuming this Court had jurisdiction
in any event.

[
33
]

Ms. Kolotyluk was, at all relevant times, and continues to be an
employee of the Edmonton Public Schools school district, also known as The
Board of Trustees of Edmonton School Division, in Alberta. Her working title is
Managing Director, Human Resources, Consulting. The Centre for Education is an
administrative office of the Edmonton Public Schools.

[
34
]

In his Application Response, the Petitioner attempts to make certain
claims against Ms. Kolotyluk and her employer. He alleges that Ms. Kolotyluk
owed a duty of good faith to ex-employees of Edmonton Public Schools. The
Petitioner did not provide any factual basis to support the proposition that there
existed any such alleged duty.

[
35
]

The Petitioner then alleges that Ms. Kolotyluk and Edmonton Public
Schools acted in bad faith. The Edmonton Public Schools are not a party to this
proceeding and no award could be made against this entity in this petition
proceeding any event. If the Petitioner intended to bring a claim against the Edmonton
Public Schools and Ms. Kolotyluk for damages for a tort, for instance, acting
in bad faith, then any such claim cannot be brought in a proceeding commenced
by a petition.

[
36
]

Further, as Edmonton Public Schools is an administrative body the
authority of which is derived from the Province of Alberta, any such proceeding
cannot be brought in British Columbia. Therefore, this claim, if it can be
called as much, has no hope of success against Ms. Kolotyluk.

[
37
]

With respect to the Langley School District, the only assertion made
is without any supportive factual statements and is a bald statement of
Charter

violations which is not available in a proceeding brought by petition. No other
relief is described against the Langley School District. There is no basis for
the Petitioner to be awarded relief against the Langley School District, and
therefore no hope of success for the Petitioner’s claim against it.

[
38
]

Further, in addition to his Application Response filed on May 5,
2023, Mr. Rashid filed a Notice of Application on May 10, 2023. In the Notice
of Application, Mr. Rashid sought orders to “strike or dismiss” the
applications of the Langley School District and Ms. Kolotyluk. However, in the
very same document at para. 1 of his “Legal Basis” section, Mr. Rashid states
that as he “has not included them in the style of the proceeding…there is no
doubt that they are not parties”. Yet, despite Mr. Rashid’s inclusion of the Langley
School District and Ms. Kolotyluk in his pleadings, Mr. Rashid then, at para. 4
of his “Legal Basis” section claims that, by seeking to remove themselves from
the litigation, they are “taking part unlawfully in the proceeding” and their
applications ought to be dismissed. This submission is wholly without merit as
it suggests that a person or entity named in litigation, even “on notice”, is barred
from responding in any form to that litigation.

[
39
]

A review of the
Rules
and its predecessor
Supreme Court
Rules
, B.C. Reg. 221/90 [the
Previous Rules
] illustrate that the
Petitioner’s above submission is incorrect.

Becoming a Party: Relevant Rules

[
40
]

Few cases have discussed this issue under the
Rules

and none have provided a clear statement of the law. The law, as a result, is
unsettled.

[
41
]

Under the
Former Rules
, a person who was
given notice of a petition proceeding and filed a response did not
automatically become a party to the proceeding:
Kitimat (District) v. B.C.
(Minister of Energy and Mines)
(2006)
2006 BCCA 562 (CanLII)
, 61 B.C.L.R. (4
th
) 295 (C.A)
(“
Kitimat
”). At para. 21 of
Kitimat
, the Court of Appeal noted:

Rules
10(5) and
51A are circular. A person who is a respondent is said to be able to file a
Form 124, and in Rule 51A that person is said to be a respondent. I think the
best reading of Rule 10(5) is that a person may file the Form 124 if he or she
is named as a respondent, or having had service under Rule10(4), have applied
to become a respondent. It is inconsistent, in my view, with the premise that
the scope of the litigation is generally with the control of the petitioners to
leave the designation of respondent within the sole control of any of the broad
class of persons who my have been served under Rule 10(4). And so it is
disorderly.

[
42
]

Under Rule 16-1(3), unless the
Rules
otherwise provide or a
court otherwise orders, a petitioner must serve a copy of the filed petition
and each filed affidavit on all persons “whose interests may be affected by the
order sought”. This provision is broader than the former reference to “a person
against whom relief is sought”.

[
43
]

Under Rule 16-1(4), a person who has been served with a copy of a
filed petition under subrule (3) must file a response and response affidavits
if that person wants to receive notice of the time and date of the hearing of
the petition.

[
44
]

Under the current Rule 16-1(1), a “petition respondent” means a
person who files a response to petition under 16-1(4). Like Rules 10(5) and
51A(2) of the
Former Rules
, this creates a circular definition of
“respondent” where to receive notice of the hearing, a person must file a
response and by filing a response that person ostensibly becomes a respondent.

The
Former Rules
(and
Kitimat)

[
45
]

Under the
Former Rules
,

Rule 10(5) required that a
“respondent who wishes to receive notice of the time and date of the hearing of
the petition or to respond to it must” file and serve “a response in Form 124”
and affidavit(s). Rule 51A defined “respondent” as “a person who has delivered
a response in Form 124”.

[
46
]

These two rules were circular: a respondent was
required to deliver a response in Form 124 and a “respondent” was defined as
being a person who had delivered a response in Form 124. The Court in
Kitimat

described that issue and came to the following conclusions:

[21]

Rules
10(5)
and 51A are circular.  A person who is a respondent is said to be able to
file a Form 124, and in Rule 51A that person is said to be a respondent.
I think the best reading of Rule 10(5) is that a person may file the Form 124
if he or she is named as a respondent, or having had service under Rule 10(4),
have applied to become a respondent.  It is inconsistent, in my view, with
the premise that the scope of the litigation is generally within the control of
the petitioners to leave the designation of respondent within the sole control
of any of the broad class of persons who may have been served under Rule
10(4).   And it is, to a degree, disorderly.

[22]

Nor do I
consider that Rule 51A gives that person status as a full party to the
proceeding in the event a person who is not yet a respondent files a Form 124,
as is here the case.  Rather, I read Rule 51A as procedural
.  The definition section, outside of s. 1 that applies to the
entire body of
Rules
, is intended, in my view, for use within that
rule only.
I do not consider that a person not yet recognized in the
proceeding as a respondent may unilaterally designate himself or herself one by
simply filing a Form 124
.

[Emphasis
added.]

The Current
Rules

[
47
]

I note that there are some differences between
the current Rules and the former rules which may affect the applicability of
Kitimat
.
As described in McLachlin and Taylor’s
British Columbia Practice
at Rule
16-1(4):

The status of a
person served with a petition but not named as a respondent and who files a
response to petition is different under the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
than it
was under SCR 1990: that person falls within the definition of a “party of
record” in Rule 1-1(1) and is entitled to fully participate in the proceeding.
This is made clear by Rule 16-1(5), which requires that a response to petition
“indicate, for each order sought, whether the petition respondent consents to,
opposes, or takes no position on the order” (Rule 16-1(5)(a)), and that a
petition respondent who opposes any of the relief sought in the petition
“briefly summarize the factual and legal bases on which the orders sought
should not be granted” (Rule 16-1(5)(b)(i)); “list the affidavits and other
documents on which the petition respondent intends to rely at the hearing (Rule
16-1(5)(b)(ii)); and “set out the petition respondent’s estimate of time the
petition will take for hearing” (Rule 16-1(5)(b)(iii)).

[
48
]

Despite these differences, the issue has been discussed at least
four times: in
Kellogg Estate (Re)
,
2014 BCSC 1541
, in
Delta Sunshine
Taxi (1972) Ltd. v. Vancouver (City)
,
2014 BCSC 2100
, in
Pierce v.
Chalice Capital Inc.
,
2016 BCSC 785
, and in
Louis v.
Civil Resolution Tribunal
,
2020 BCSC 2061
.
Unfortunately, each of these cases has deficiencies that mean they are not
particularly thorough statements of the law:

•

In
Kellogg
, the Court did not discuss and
does not appear to have been referred to
Kitimat
.

•

In
Delta Sunshine
, the parties agreed
that merely filing a response would not make a person a respondent so the Court
did not provide detailed analysis on the point.

•

Pierce
dealt with
a slightly different situation where the company at issue had not been served
or put on notice of the petition but filed a response in a unilateral effort to
become a respondent.

•

In
Louis
, the corporation was served by
the petitioner as “a person whose interests may be affected” and filed a
response to petition, but also brought an application to be granted full party
status under Rule 6-2(7).

Kellogg

[
49
]

In
Kellogg Estate
, Justice Gray provided Supplementary
Reasons for Judgment and Corrigendum to
Kellogg Estate (Re)
,
2014 BCSC
2292
. It appears the corrections were made to, among other things, list certain
persons as respondents in the cover page’s style of cause. In the initial
petition, the petitioner “did not name any petitioners or respondents, but
stated that it was ‘on notice to’” a few individuals”: at para. 18. In the
Supplementary Reasons, the Court discussed the effect of filing a response to a
petition after not being named as respondents:

[15]      Rule 16-1(4) requires petition
respondents to indicate their position on the relief sought and summarize the
factual and legal bases on which the petition respondent opposes the relief
sought. Rule 16-1(8) requires the petitioner to give each petition respondent
notice of the hearing.

[16]      As a result,
a person can learn
of a petition, file a response, and thereby become a petition respondent
entitled to notice of the hearing, whether or not that person is named in the
style of cause as a respondent
.

[17]      In my view, there is no material
difference between a person “whose interests may be affected by the order
sought” (as stated in Rule 16-1(3) regarding service) and a person “against
whom relief is sought” (as stated in Form 66).
That is because the decision
will ordinarily be binding on everyone who received proper notice of the
petition, and so the petitioner effectively seeks the relief against everyone
served that they are bound by the result of the petition
. The point of
involving others in the petition proceedings is to ensure that they have notice
that the court will deal with an issue that may affect them, and to give them
the opportunity to provide evidence and argument to the court. A petitioner’s
decision about who should be served with the petition is not a final decision
about who has standing to participate in the court process and is bound by the
result, but as a practical matter it is often determinative of who has
knowledge of the proceeding and is bound by the result.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
50
]

As noted, the Court did not discuss and does not appear to have been
referred to
Kitimat
.

Delta Sunshine

[
51
]

On the other hand, in the slightly more recent
Delta Sunshine
,
the Court referenced
Kitimat

and noted the applicants and petitioners
agreed that merely filing a response did not make a person a respondent or
party:

[11]      It
was agreed by both the applicants and the petitioners
that
if the applicants were to be served under Rule 16-1(3) and if the applicants
filed a response pursuant to Rule 16-1(4), they would not be made a respondent
or a party in the sense that they might have status as a full party to the
proceeding
. As described in
Kitimat (District) v. Alcan Inc.
,
2006
BCCA 562
at paras.
20-23
(
Kitimat
),
service under Rule 10 (now Rule 16-1(3)) is broadly
interpreted to include a person who “may” be affected by an order sought and is
not intended to give a person status as a full party to the proceeding. The
person must apply for party status under present Rule 6-2(7).

Pierce

[
52
]

The Court in
Pierce
was concerned with the slightly different
situation of a company who was neither named as a respondent by the petitioner
nor served by the petitioner, but who wanted to be involved in the petition and
therefore filed a response to petition. The company wanted to automatically be
heard on the petition as a result of its filing a response, but the Court held
that it had to be formally added as a party under Rule 6-2(7), based on
Kitimat
.

[
53
]

As the Court was not dealing “with the situation of a person who is
given notice of a petition by the petitioner but not named as a respondent” and
as “the parties have not addressed” the differences to this regard between the
former and current rules, it declined to comment on whether a person given
notice of a petition who files a response becomes a respondent. That said,
there is obiter which may be instructive as it relates to both
Delta
Sunshine
,
Kellogg
, and the role of
Kitimat
:

[35]      As a first
point, the Court of Appeal in
Kitimat (District) v. Alcan Inc.
,

2006 BCCA
562
at paras.
20-23
(
Kitimat
), made it clear that a
party
cannot unilaterally become a respondent to a petition, if not otherwise named
in it as a respondent, simply by filing a response to the petition
.
Instead, if a party who has not been named as a respondent by the petitioner
seeks to be added as a respondent, that party must either apply to be added as
a respondent or apply to intervene.

[36]      I note
that
Kitimat
also dealt with the situation of a person who is
given notice of a petition by the petitioner but not named as a respondent. We
are not dealing with that situation here as Mr. Pierce did not give 490
notice of the petition.

[37]      On that
question, the status of a person served with a petition, the
Kitimat
decision
was made under a predecessor Rule, R. 10.

[38]      There are some
important differences as between R. 10 and the current R. 16-1.
The
parties have not addressed these differences and so I decline to comment on
whether
the reasoning of
Kitimat

applies to persons given
formal notice of a petition but not named as a respondent in it
.

[39]

It could be argued that the implicit conclusion
reached
in
Delta Sunshine Taxi (1972) Ltd. v. Vancouver (City)
,
2014 BCSC 2100
, was that all of
the
reasoning in
Kitimat

remains applicable to petition
proceedings commenced pursuant to R. 16‑1
. That case applied
Kitimat
to
the situation before it and concluded that a party that wished to become a
party to a petition had to apply to be added as a respondent under
R. 6-2(7) or apply to intervene. I do note however that this position was
not contested and instead appeared to be a point of agreement by the parties,
as noted at para. 11 of
Delta Sunshine Taxi
.

[Emphasis added.]

[
54
]

The Court then noted that
Kellogg
contradicted
Delta
Sunshine
before noting that “the Court in
Kellogg
appears not to
have been referred to the decision in
Kitimat
: at para.
41
.

Louis

[
55
]

In
Louis
, a strata corporation was served
with a copy of the petition and filed a petition response. While the court
noted at para. 32 that “[i]t would seem that on this basis alone, the Strata
Corporation qualifies as a party of record”, it pointed to
Kitimat
to
explain why the Strata Corporation also brought an application under Rule
6-2(7) to be made a ‘full party’:

[33]

However, as
explained in
Kitimat (District) v. Alcan Inc.
,
2006 BCCA
562
at para.
22-23
, service under what is now Rule 16-1(3) and the
filing of a response under what is now Rule 16-1(4) makes a person a party of
record but does not necessarily confer the status of “a full party”. It is not
uncommon in judicial review proceedings for persons who wish to be heard to be
joined as “intervenors”, rather than as “respondents” having “full party”
status. Simply being served with the petition on the basis that one’s interests
“may be affected” is not necessarily enough to confer the full rights of
participation enjoyed by a petition respondent.

[34]      To
address this concern, the Strata Corporation has brought a formal application
to be added as a party under Rule 6-2(7). Under Rule 16-1(18) the Court has
discretion to apply Rule 6-2(7) in a petition proceeding, and I consider it
necessary to do so in this case, in order to determine what role the Strata
Corporation should play in the proceeding, specifically whether its role should
be limited to that of an intervenor, or whether it should be granted the full
party status of a respondent.

[
56
]

The Court did not mention
Kellogg
,
Delta Sunshine
, nor

Pierce
in its reasons.

[
57
]

Ultimately on this point, I follow the notation in
Pierce

at
para.
39
that
Delta Sunshine
implicitly concluded that
Kitimat
applies
to petition proceedings under Rule 16-1. Ms. Kolotyluk and the Langley School
District were not made full parties by merely filing a response.

Striking Pleadings and Removal of
the “On Notice” Entities

[
58
]

Rule 9-5(1) of the
Rules
sets out the
Court’s authority to strike out pleadings, petitions, or other documents:

… At any stage of a proceeding, the court
may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading,
petition or other document on the ground that

(a)  it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b)  it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)  it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, or

(d)  it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
59
]

Rules
9-5(1)(b) and 9-5(1)(d) are of particular
relevance in this case.

[
60
]

Under Rule 9-5(1)(b), a pleading may be unnecessary or vexatious
if it would serve no useful purpose or would be a waste of the court’s time and
public resources:
Nevsun Resources Ltd. v. Araya
,
2020 SCC 5
at
para.
65
,
citing
Willow v. Chong
,
2013 BCSC 1083
at
para.
20
.
In
Willow
, Justice Fisher (as she
then was) described the principles relevant to Rule 9-5(1)(b):

[20]

Under
Rule 9-5(1)(b)
, a pleading is unnecessary or vexatious
if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action, if it does
not advance any claim known in law, where it is obvious that an action cannot
succeed, or where it would serve no useful purpose and would be a waste of the
court’s time and public resources:
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc.
v Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] BCJ No. 2160 (SC);
Skender
v Farley
,
2007 BCCA 629
. If a pleading is so confusing that it is difficult
to understand what is pleaded, it may also be unnecessary, frivolous or
vexatious. An application under this sub-rule may be supported by evidence.

[
61
]

With respect to Rule 9-5(1)(d), in
Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E.,
Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
, the Supreme Court of Canada explained that the
doctrine of abuse of process engages the court’s inherent jurisdiction to
prevent the misuse of its procedure in a way that would be manifestly unfair to
a litigant or would otherwise bring the administration of justice into
disrepute. Further, that the doctrine has expanded “beyond the strict
parameters of
res judicata
” to include policy grounds such as preserving
the courts’ and the litigants’ resources: at para. 38.
In
Willow
, Fisher
J. also explained the relevant considerations with respect to Rule 9-5(1)(d):

[21]

Abuse of
process under Rule 9-5(1)(d) or the court’s inherent discretion is a flexible
doctrine. It allows the court to prevent a claim from proceeding where to do so
would violate principles of judicial economy, consistency, finality and the
integrity of the administration of justice. A claim may be struck where it is a
collateral attack on an administrative decision that is subject to appeal or
judicial review:
Cimaco International Sales Inc. v British Columbia
,

2010 BCCA 342
;
Stephen v HMTQ
,
2008 BCSC 1656
;
Varzeliotis
v British Columbia
,
2007 BCSC 620
;
Gemex Developments Corp. v City
of Coquitlam
,
2002 BCSC 412
;
Berscheid v Ensign
,
1999 CanLII 6494 (BC SC)
, [1999] BCJ
No. 1172 (SC). A claim may also be struck as an abuse of process where it
is an attempt to re-litigate an issue that has already been decided:
Toronto
(City) v Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE), Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
.

[
62
]

The Petitioner has brought a proceeding against the applicants “on
notice” and they are admittedly not parties to that proceeding. There are no
rules of this Court that permit or authorize the Petitioner to proceed by
petition on an “on notice” basis. The Petitioner submits that by filing a
response to the petition and bringing this application to strike references to
these “non-parties”, they have become “parties”.

[
63
]

This argument by the Petitioner has no merit. If this proceeding was
allowed by the Court, the situation remains that there are no allegations of
fact which could support any claim against either applicant. In other words, if
the claims of the Petitioner were permitted to proceed as currently advanced,
no order nor judgment could be rendered against the applicants in any event.
This proceeding would be a complete waste of this Court’s time, and a vexatious
and unnecessary expenditure of valuable and limited public resources.

[
64
]

The current applicants are entitled to be protected by this Court
from the vexatious abuse of the Court’s processes: see
Household Trust Co.
v. Golden Horse Farms Inc.
(1992), 65 B.C.L.R. (2d) 355,
1992 CanLII 420
(C.A.)
at para.
28
, leave to appeal to SCC ref’d, 2548 (19 November 1992). The
foregoing decision has been followed repeatedly in our courts: see e.g.,
Universe
v. Forslund
,
2021 BCSC 812
at para.
98
, aff’d
2022 BCCA 202
.

I am well aware that the Court should be cautious in the exercise of
this protective jurisdiction.

[
65
]

This Court also adopts and relies upon the reasons expressed by Edelmann
J. in the Judicial Review of the HRT Decision involving Mr. Rashid, which
decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal of British Columbia, as noted above.
The reference to the two parties being put on notice in the circumstances of
this proceeding is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous
or vexatious and the repetition of the same type of claims in several files
noted above where there is no hope of success can serve no useful purpose and
is a waste of court resources.

Vexatious Proceedings

[
66
]

The court has the power, under
s. 18
of the
Supreme
Court Act
, to order that a person may not institute legal proceedings
without leave of the court:

18
If, on application by any person, the court is satisfied that a
person has habitually, persistently and without reasonable grounds, instituted
vexatious legal proceedings in the Supreme Court or in the Provincial Court
against the same or different persons, the court may, after hearing that person
or giving the person an opportunity to be heard, order that a legal proceeding
must not, without leave of the court, be instituted by that person in any
court.

[
67
]

While the Langley School District applied for a vexatious proceeding
order, the Supreme Court also has the ability via its inherent jurisdiction to
control its own process to make such orders regarding vexatious litigants:
Gichuru
v. Pallai
,
2018 BCCA 78
at para.
74
; see also
Foy v. Tranfo
,
2011
BCCA 494
at para.
12
.

[
68
]

To ground an order under
s. 18
of the
Supreme Court Act
, the
proceedings must, first, be “vexatious” in the sense that they are “without
reasonable grounds”:
British Columbia (Public Guardian and Trustee) v. Brown
,

2002 BCSC 1152
at para.
47
. Second, “there must be a knowing and deliberate
repetition or continuation of the vexatious conduct”:
Brown
at para.
48
.
This is an objective determination—whether a reasonable person in the same
circumstances would have believed the conduct was vexatious:
Brown
at
para.
48
.

[
69
]

In
Holland (Guardian ad litem of) v. Marshall
,

2010 BCCA 243
at paras.
12–15
, Justice Groberman accepted and applied a set of
non-exhaustive principles in respect of vexatious proceedings originally
outlined by Justice Henry in
Re Lang Michener and Fabian
(1987), 59 O.R.
(2d) 353,
1987 CanLII 172 (H.C.J.)
. The principles were summarized in
Pearlman
v. Insurance Corporation of British Columbia
,
2010 BCCA 362
at para.
5
:

(a)     the bringing of one or more actions
to determine an issue which has already been determined by a court of competent
jurisdiction constitutes a vexatious proceeding;

(b)      where it is obvious that an action
cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no possible good, or if no
reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain relief, the action is
vexatious;

(c)   vexatious actions include those
brought for an improper purpose, including the harassment and oppression of
other parties by multifarious proceedings brought for purposes other than the
assertion of legitimate rights;

(d)        it is a general characteristic of
vexatious proceedings that grounds and issues raised tend to be rolled forward
into subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented, often with actions
brought against the lawyers who have acted for or against the litigant in
earlier proceedings;

(e)        in determining whether
proceedings are vexatious, the court must look at the whole history of the
matter and not just whether there was originally a good cause of action;

(f)        the failure of the person
instituting the proceedings to pay the costs of unsuccessful proceedings is one
factor to be considered in determining whether proceedings are vexatious;

(g)        the
respondent's conduct in persistently taking unsuccessful appeals from judicial
decisions can be considered vexatious conduct of legal proceedings.

[
70
]

Mr. Rashid was provided with multiple, clear warnings in the Alberta
Court and in Judicial Review of the HRT Decision of Edelmann J. strengthened by
the subsequent decision of the British Columbia Court of Appeal. He has not
heeded those warnings nor followed the courts’ advice. In these circumstances,
no reasonable litigant could reasonably expect, by repeating the same type of
claims, to obtain relief. For instance, bringing this “on notice” proceeding
against Ms. Kolotyluk, where there is no jurisdiction in British Columbia, is
simple harassment. This Court is satisfied, consistent with the language in
Holland

at para.
14
, that this Petitioner has “
engaged in vexatious
proceedings on a habitual and persistent basis and without reasonable cause”.

[
71
]

Given this finding, and the repeated involvement of these parties in
vexatious proceedings by the Petitioner, the Applicants are entitled to special
costs of this proceeding throughout payable by the Petitioner, after
assessment.
